messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Elijah’s younger brother collapsed in their Atlanta kitchen, the sudden stillness was broken only by the frantic wail of approaching ambulances. He had dialed emergency services with shaking hands, waiting in the hallway as the flashing lights washed over the peeling paint, until the paramedics shook their heads. The event left him with no gradual goodbyes, only the stark, unblinking images of his brother’s pale face and the hollow finality of the stretcher’s wheels. In the months that followed, Elijah, a fifty-five-year-old Black American painter, found his carefully ordered life unraveling. The moment a siren passed his high-rise scaffold or a foreman mentioned a crew member’s recent bereavement, his shoulders locked and his chest tightened into a rigid plate of dread. These environmental cues did not merely remind him of the past; they actively threw him into a state of raw physical readiness, even as they surfaced the same vivid, freezing pictures and overwhelming sorrow that had first broken him. Each time the memories of his brother’s stillness rose, they confirmed his deepest fears: he felt like a stranger to his own hands, permanently cut off from the community he once knew, and certain that his life had been irreparably shattered. The belief that his world was ruined made the mere thought of dusk unbearable, his body bracing for collapse before the sun even dipped below the horizon. That same conviction pulled up the fragmented images and hollow grief he tried to outrun, while the fear of his own fractured state kept his ears wide open for any hint of loss or emergency, turning ordinary job-site chatter into a relentless threat scan. He came to believe that his own nervous system was fundamentally broken, a realization that only made the hallway flashes more frequent. The sudden rush of those visual memories and the weight of his grief instantly dropped his heart rate into a frantic rhythm, leaving his muscles coiled and ready to bolt. Some mornings, he wakes up drenched in the visceral panic of that hallway without a single picture in his mind, just the raw, body-shaking certainty that disaster has returned. He began to describe the event not as a story, but as a physical weight that crushed his chest whenever he tried to speak of it, confirming his isolation from everyone else. Replaying those moments only deepened his conviction that he was unmoored from his former self, while the memories themselves acted as magnets, pulling his attention back to every passing wail, every hushed conversation about sudden hospital stays, and every sudden workplace deadline that mimicked the original chaos. His constant bodily readiness and the way he patrolled his own living room at night prevented him from resting, which in turn left his mind wide open to the intrusive pictures and the crushing grief that followed. This perpetual state of alertness also forced him to retreat from the scaffolding, scanning every corner for emergency vehicles or signs of collapse, until he could no longer hold the physical demands of his own livelihood or maintain the quiet routines his wife had come to rely on. He now avoids lifting heavy brushes or standing on ladders, his hands trembling at the mere suggestion of urgency. Now, sitting in a therapist’s office, he admits that the fear of another sudden loss has finally overwhelmed his need to endure alone. He fears that if he looks too closely at the wreckage, he will lose the last fragments of the man he used to be, yet he hopes that by naming the storm, he might finally learn to rest in his own home.
